title: Text & List Semantics 📝
description: Paragraphs, lists, emphasis, and blockquotes – how they communicate meaning to assistive tech.

slides.title: The Building Blocks of Text 🧱
slides.content:
Text elements convey **meaning**, not just style. * `

` – paragraph * `` – strong importance (bold by default) * `` – emphasis (italic by default) * `

` – quoted content with citation Screen readers may announce these semantics (e.g., "quote").

quizData.question: What is the difference between `<b>` and `<strong>`?
quizData.explanation: Screen readers may emphasise `<strong>` but treat `<b>` as ordinary text. Use semantic versions for accessibility.

slides.title: Lists Are More Than Bullets 📋
slides.content:
Lists convey a relationship between items:

* `<ul>` – unordered list
* `<ol>` – ordered list (numbered)
* `<dl>` – description list (terms + definitions)

Screen readers announce the number of items and current item index, helping users understand structure.

slides.title: Description List Example
slides.codeSnippet:
<dl>
  <dt>Accessibility</dt>
  <dd>The practice of making websites usable for everyone.</dd>
</dl>

quizData.question: What does a screen reader typically announce when entering a `<ul>` with three items?
quizData.explanation: Screen readers announce the type and number of items, allowing users to understand the grouping.

slides.title: Quotes & Citations 💬
slides.content:
Use `<blockquote>` for block‑level quotes and `<q>` for inline quotes. Include the `cite` attribute or a citation element.

* `<blockquote cite="...">`
* `<q>` – automatically adds quotation marks (depending on language).

Screen readers may announce "quote" and the citation URL if linked.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Don't Fake Lists with Dashes `- Item 1
- Item 2` has no semantic meaning. Always use `
    ` or `
      `.
